items.new: There was a circumstance that at first glance seemed to entangle his delirious but still methodical scheme. But perhaps it did not in reality. Though the gregarious sperm whales have their regular seasons for particular grounds, you generally cannot conclude that the herds that haunted such-and-such a latitude or longitude this year, say, will turn out to be identically the same as those found there the season before — though there are peculiar and unquestionable cases where the contrary has proved true. In general, the same remark applies, only within narrower limits, to the solitaries and hermits among the mature, aged sperm whales. So although Moby Dick had in a former year been seen, for example, on what is called the Seychelle ground in the Indian Ocean, or in Volcano Bay on the Japanese coast, it did not follow that if the Pequod visited either of those spots at any later corresponding season, she would infallibly meet him there. The same was true of some other feeding grounds where he had at times shown himself. But all these seemed only his casual stopping-places and ocean-inns, so to speak, not his places of long residence. And where Ahab's chances of achieving his object have been spoken of so far, the reference has only been to whatever wayside, preliminary, extra prospects were his before a particular fixed time or place was reached — when all possibilities would become probabilities, and, as Ahab fondly thought, every possibility the next thing to a certainty. That particular time and place were joined in the one technical phrase: the Season-on-the-Line (the Line being the equator). For there and then, for several consecutive years, Moby Dick had been periodically sighted, lingering in those waters for a while, just as the sun in its annual round loiters for a predicted interval in any one sign of the Zodiac. It was there, too, that most of the deadly encounters with the white whale had taken place; there the very waves were storied with his deeds; there also was that tragic spot where the monomaniac old man had found the awful motive for his vengeance. But with the cautious thoroughness and unresting vigilance with which Ahab threw his brooding soul into this unfaltering hunt, he would not allow himself to rest all his hopes on the one crowning fact just mentioned, however flattering it might be to those hopes; nor, in the sleeplessness of his vow, could he so calm his unquiet heart as to put off all searching in the meantime.

items.new: Often, when he was driven from his hammock by exhausting and intolerably vivid dreams of the night — dreams which took up his own intense thoughts of the day and carried them on amid a clash of frenzies, whirling them round and round and round in his blazing brain until the very throbbing of his life-spot became unbearable anguish — and when, as was sometimes the case, these spiritual throes heaved his being up from its foundations, and a chasm seemed to open in him, from which forked flames and lightnings shot up, and accursed fiends beckoned him to leap down among them — when this hell within him yawned beneath him, a wild cry would be heard through the ship, and with glaring eyes Ahab would burst from his stateroom, as though escaping from a bed that was on fire. Yet these outbursts, perhaps, instead of being the irrepressible symptoms of some hidden weakness, or of fright at his own resolve, were only the plainest signs of its intensity. For at such times crazy Ahab, the scheming, unappeasably steadfast hunter of the white whale — this Ahab who had gone to his hammock — was not the agent that made him burst from it again in horror. That agent was the eternal, living principle, or soul, in him; and in sleep, being for the time separated from the characterizing mind, which at other times used it as its outer vehicle or agent, it spontaneously sought to escape from the scorching nearness of the frantic thing of which, for the time, it was no longer an integral part. But since the mind does not exist unless joined with the soul, it must have been that in Ahab's case, as he yielded up all his thoughts and fancies to his one supreme purpose, that purpose, by the sheer stubbornness of its own will, forced itself, against gods and devils, into a kind of self-assumed, independent being of its own. Indeed, it could grimly live and burn while the common vitality to which it was joined fled horror-stricken from the unbidden and unfathered birth. Therefore the tormented spirit that glared out of bodily eyes, when what seemed Ahab rushed from his room, was for the time only an emptied thing, a formless sleepwalking being — a ray of living light, to be sure, but without an object to color, and therefore a blankness in itself. God help you, old man, your thoughts have created a creature in you; and he whose intense thinking thus makes him a Prometheus — a vulture feeds upon that heart forever; that vulture the very creature he creates.

He went ashore there, joined a discovery party, and made his way far into the interior, where he traveled for nearly two years, often endangered by serpents, savages, tigers, poisonous miasmas, and all the other common perils of wandering in the heart of unknown regions. This man and this whale came together again, and the one vanquished the other. I say that I myself have known three instances like this: that is, in two of them I saw the whales struck, and after the second attack saw the two irons, with their respective marks cut in them, afterwards taken from the dead fish. In the three-year instance, it so happened that I was in the boat both times, first and last, and the last time I clearly recognized a peculiar sort of huge mole under the whale's eye which I had observed there three years before. I say three years, but I am pretty sure it was more than that. Here, then, are three instances whose truth I personally know; but I have heard of many other instances from people whose truthfulness in the matter there is no good reason to doubt.

items.new: First: In the year 1820 the ship Essex, Captain Pollard, of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean. One day she saw spouts, lowered her boats, and gave chase to a shoal of sperm whales. Before long several of the whales were wounded, when suddenly a very large whale, escaping from the boats, broke out of the shoal and bore straight down upon the ship. Dashing his forehead against her hull, he stove her in so badly that in less than "ten minutes" she settled down and fell over. Not a surviving plank of her has been seen since. After the most severe exposure, part of the crew reached land in their boats. When he had at last returned home, Captain Pollard sailed once more for the Pacific in command of another ship, but the gods shipwrecked him again on unknown rocks and breakers; for the second time his ship was utterly lost, and, at once forswearing the sea, he has never tempted it since. Captain Pollard lives in Nantucket to this day. I have seen Owen Chace, who was chief mate of the Essex at the time of the tragedy; I have read his plain and faithful narrative; I have talked with his son; and all this within a few miles of the scene of the catastrophe.

items.new: I might go on with several more examples, known to me one way or another, of the great power and malice the sperm whale at times shows. In more than one instance he has been known not only to chase the attacking boats back to their ships, but to pursue the ship itself and hold out for a long time against all the lances hurled at him from its decks. The English ship Pusie Hall can tell a story on that score; and as for his strength, let me say that there have been cases where the lines attached to a running sperm whale have, in a calm, been transferred to the ship and made fast there, the whale towing her great hull through the water as a horse walks off with a cart. Again, it is very often observed that if the sperm whale, once struck, is given time to rally, he then acts not so often with blind rage as with willful, deliberate designs of destruction against his pursuers; and it says something eloquent about his character that, when attacked, he will often open his mouth and hold it in that dreadful gape for several minutes on end. But I must be content with only one more, concluding illustration — a remarkable and most significant one, from which you will not fail to see not only that the most marvelous event in this book is corroborated by plain facts of the present day, but that these marvels (like all marvels) are mere repetitions of the ages; so that for the millionth time we say amen with Solomon — truly, there is nothing new under the sun.

items.new: Now, in this history of his, Procopius mentions that, during the term of his prefecture at Constantinople, a great sea-monster was captured in the neighboring Propontis, or Sea of Marmora, after it had destroyed vessels at intervals in those waters for more than fifty years. A fact set down like this in substantial history cannot easily be denied. Nor is there any reason it should be. What precise species this sea-monster was is not mentioned. But since he destroyed ships, as well as for other reasons, he must have been a whale; and I am strongly inclined to think a sperm whale. And I will tell you why. For a long time I imagined that the sperm whale had always been unknown in the Mediterranean and the deep waters connecting with it. Even now I am certain that those seas are not, and perhaps never can be, in the present constitution of things, a place he habitually resorts to in herds. But further investigations have recently proved to me that in modern times there have been isolated instances of the sperm whale's presence in the Mediterranean. I am told, on good authority, that on the Barbary coast a Commodore Davis of the British navy found the skeleton of a sperm whale. Now, since a vessel of war passes readily through the Dardanelles, a sperm whale could by the same route pass out of the Mediterranean into the Propontis.

items.new: In the Propontis, as far as I can learn, none of that peculiar substance called brit — the food of the right whale — is to be found. But I have every reason to believe that the food of the sperm whale — squid or cuttlefish — lurks at the bottom of that sea, because large creatures of that sort, though by no means the largest, have been found at its surface. If, then, you properly put these statements together and reason on them a bit, you will clearly see that, according to all human reasoning, Procopius's sea-monster, which for half a century stove in the ships of a Roman Emperor, must in all probability have been a sperm whale.

items.new: To accomplish his object Ahab had to use tools; and of all tools used in the shadow of the moon, men are the most apt to get out of order. He knew, for example, that however magnetic his ascendancy over Starbuck was in some respects, that ascendancy did not cover the whole spiritual man, any more than mere bodily superiority implies intellectual mastery; for to the purely spiritual, the intellectual stands only in a sort of bodily relation. Starbuck's body and Starbuck's coerced will were Ahab's, so long as Ahab kept his magnet at Starbuck's brain; still, he knew that for all this the chief mate in his soul abhorred his captain's quest, and if he could, would joyfully cut himself loose from it, or even thwart it. It might be a long time before the White Whale was seen. During that long interval Starbuck would always be liable to fall into open relapses of rebellion against his captain's leadership, unless some ordinary, prudential, circumstantial influences were brought to bear on him. Not only that, but the subtle insanity of Ahab concerning Moby Dick was nowhere more significantly shown than in his superlative sense and shrewdness in foreseeing that, for the present, the hunt should somehow be stripped of the strange imaginative impiety that naturally clothed it; that the full terror of the voyage must be kept back in the dim background (for few men's courage can hold out against long brooding unrelieved by action); and that when they stood their long night watches, his officers and men must have some nearer things to think about than Moby Dick. For however eagerly and impetuously the savage crew had hailed the announcement of his quest, all sailors of every sort are more or less capricious and unreliable — they live in the changing outer weather, and they breathe in its fickleness — and when they are kept on for some object remote and blank in the pursuit, however much it promises life and passion in the end, it is above all necessary that temporary interests and occupations should intervene and hold them healthily suspended for the final dash.

items.new: Nor did Ahab forget another thing. In times of strong emotion mankind scorns all base considerations; but such times are fleeting. The permanent, constitutional condition of the manufactured man, thought Ahab, is sordidness. Granted that the White Whale fully stirs the hearts of this savage crew of mine, and, playing around their savageness, even breeds a certain generous knight-errantry in them — still, while they chase Moby Dick for the love of it, they must also have food for their more common, everyday appetites. For even the lofty, chivalric Crusaders of old were not content to cross two thousand miles of land to fight for their holy sepulchre without committing burglaries, picking pockets, and gaining other pious perks along the way. Had they been held strictly to their one final and romantic object, too many would have turned from that final and romantic object in disgust. I will not strip these men, thought Ahab, of all hope of cash — yes, cash. They may scorn cash now; but let some months go by with no prospect of it in view, and then this same dormant cash, suddenly mutinying in them, would soon cashier Ahab — dismiss him from his command.

items.new: There was yet another precautionary motive, more closely related to Ahab personally. Having revealed the prime but private purpose of the Pequod's voyage — impulsively, it is probable, and perhaps somewhat prematurely — Ahab was now fully aware that in doing so he had indirectly laid himself open to the unanswerable charge of usurpation; and with perfect impunity, both moral and legal, his crew, if they were so inclined and able to carry it out, could refuse all further obedience to him, and even take the command from him by force. Ahab must of course have been most anxious to protect himself from even the barest hint of a charge of usurpation, and from the possible consequences of such a suppressed feeling gaining ground. That protection could lie only in his own dominating brain and heart and hand, backed by a careful, closely calculating attention to every minute atmospheric influence to which his crew could possibly be subjected.

items.new: I was Queequeg's attendant, or page, while he was busy at the mat. As I kept passing the filling, or woof, of marline back and forth between the long yarns of the warp, using my own hand as the shuttle, and as Queequeg, standing sideways, every now and then slid his heavy oaken sword between the threads and, idly looking off at the water, carelessly and unthinkingly drove every yarn home — I say, so strange a dreaminess reigned then over all the ship and all the sea, broken only by the intermittent dull sound of the sword, that it seemed as if this were the Loom of Time, and I myself a shuttle mechanically weaving and weaving away at the Fates. There lay the fixed threads of the warp, subject to only one single, ever-returning, unchanging vibration, and that vibration just enough to allow other threads to be interwoven crosswise with its own. This warp seemed necessity; and here, I thought, with my own hand I ply my own shuttle and weave my own destiny into these unalterable threads. Meanwhile Queequeg's impulsive, indifferent sword sometimes hit the woof slantwise, or crookedly, or strongly, or weakly, as the case might be, and by this difference in the concluding blow produced a corresponding contrast in the final look of the finished fabric. This savage's sword, I thought, which in the end shapes and fashions both warp and woof — this easy, indifferent sword must be chance — yes, chance, free will, and necessity, in no way incompatible, all working together, interwoven. The straight warp of necessity, not to be swerved from its ultimate course — its every alternating vibration, indeed, only tending toward that; free will, still free to ply her shuttle between given threads; and chance, though restrained in its play within the straight lines of necessity, and directed sideways in its motions by free will — though thus prescribed to by both, chance rules each of them by turns, and has the last, shaping blow at events.

items.new: Thus we were weaving and weaving away when I started at a sound so strange, long-drawn, and musically wild and unearthly that the ball of free will dropped from my hand, and I stood gazing up at the clouds from which that voice dropped like a wing. High aloft in the crosstrees was that mad Gay-Header, Tashtego. His body was reaching eagerly forward, his hand stretched out like a wand, and at brief, sudden intervals he continued his cries. To be sure, the same sound was perhaps at that very moment being heard all over the seas, from hundreds of whalemen's lookouts perched just as high in the air; but from few of those lungs could that familiar old cry have drawn such a marvelous cadence as from Tashtego the Indian's.

items.new: The ship was now kept away from the wind, and she went gently rolling before it. Since Tashtego reported that the whales had gone down heading to leeward, we confidently expected to see them again directly ahead of our bows. For that singular cunning the Sperm Whale at times shows — when, sounding (diving deep) with his head in one direction, he nevertheless mills round while hidden beneath the surface and swiftly swims off the opposite way — this deceitfulness of his could not be at work now; for there was no reason to suppose that the fish Tashtego had seen had been alarmed in any way, or indeed knew we were anywhere near. One of the men chosen as shipkeepers — that is, those not assigned to the boats — had by this time relieved the Indian at the mainmast head. The sailors at the fore and mizzen had come down; the line tubs were fixed in their places; the cranes were thrust out; the mainyard was backed; and the three boats swung over the sea like three samphire baskets over high cliffs. Outside the bulwarks their eager crews clung to the rail with one hand, while one foot was poised expectantly on the gunwale. So looks the long line of a man-of-war's men about to throw themselves aboard an enemy's ship.
